question: Are customers describing the same underlying problem in different ways?

answer.answer_markdown:
**Yes - and that is exactly why the problem looks smaller than it is.** The biggest single issue in the book is a fraud or transaction dispute being denied without the evidence ever being looked at. It runs through 394 of the 4,425 contacts, 8.9% of everything that came in - and those 394 contacts are worded 397 different ways. Effectively no two customers describe it the same way: one writes about a stolen card used at festival stalls with no cameras, one about a timeshare company that was given 18 months to act, one about a document upload page that only reopened after the weekend, one about a card chip the bank insisted could not be cloned. Same failure, four vocabularies.

The second largest issue behaves the same way: an account closed or restricted with no reason given, 314 contacts, 7.1% of the book, and 320 distinct wordings. It arrives as a frozen investment portfolio, as cards terminated the same day a mother sent a family transfer, as a branch that would not state the time and date of the closure, as an email to a small business that nobody could explain. The words share almost nothing; the underlying failure is one back-office decision nobody can explain to the customer.

That near one-to-one ratio of wordings to contacts holds right down the top ten - 397 wordings over 394 contacts at the top, 99 over 97 at the tenth. It means keyword rules, tag lists and canned dispositions cannot find these customers: there is no shared phrase to search for. It also means the volume is invisible where it lands. The dispute-evidence theme alone spans 6 products and 41 states, so every product owner and every regional queue sees a handful of unrelated-looking cases rather than the single 394-contact failure they are all part of.

What to do with it: stop routing and counting by keyword or by product, and give these two themes a named owner each - one for deny only after the available evidence has actually been pulled, one for never close an account without a reason the front line can state. Then track the fix by whether the theme contact count falls, not by whether a particular phrase stops appearing, because the phrase was never the same twice.

quotes.why: Same theme, described as the bank being unable to produce a signed authorization - no dispute or fraud vocabulary at all.

quotes.quote: call Chase bank back to give them polic report number and to ask them to stop payment because transaction is still pending but they said they can not do that.
quotes.why: Same theme, described as a refusal to stop a still-pending payment after a police report was supplied.

quotes.why: Same theme again, described as a dispute clock running out after the bank set an 18-month wait - no keyword links it to the two above.

quotes.why: Closed-with-no-reason theme, described as a family transfer arriving and the accounts being terminated the same day.

quotes.quote: Chase refused to put the time and date of the account closure.
quotes.why: Same closure theme, described only as a refusal to state the time and date of the closure.

quotes.quote: JP Morgan Chase has locked access to my digital portfolio to claim that I am somehow defrauding them. I simply want access to my account, and they are requesting information that does not exist in order to gain access.
quotes.why: Same closure theme again, described as a locked investment portfolio and a demand for information that does not exist.

charts.title: Themes ranked by how many different ways customers word them

caveats: This is a complaint corpus: it is the unhappy end of the contact mix, not the whole voice of the customer.
Complaint dates lag the contact they describe, so the most recent weeks are still filling in.

Wordings are counted from the extracted issue statement of each contact, so the count of distinct wordings tracks the count of contacts by construction; the finding is that those wordings share no common phrasing, not the count itself.
Theme membership comes from a model grouping the contacts, so a small number of edge cases in either theme may be grouped generously.
followups: Which of the 397 wordings of the dispute-evidence theme are being routed to the wrong queue today, and what would correct routing cost?
Does the closed-with-no-reason theme cluster around particular triggers such as large incoming transfers, and would stating a reason at closure reduce repeat contacts?

confidence.badge: broad pattern · 394 calls · 24 months · 6 products · 41 states

payload.name: list_themes
payload.summary: 10 rows over 4425 calls in scope; Fraud dispute denied without reviewing the evidence (394), Account closed and the bank will not say why (314), Processing mistake stays uncorrected after being reported (226)

sql.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS n, MIN(c.date) AS d0, MAX(c.date) AS d1 FROM calls c WHERE 1=1

SELECT th.theme_id, th.name, th.problem_statement, th.root_cause, th.polarity, th.driver_category, th.n_wordings, th.n_products, COALESCE(th.grouping_quality, 'ok') AS grouping_quality, th.first_seen_week, es.status AS status_at_as_of, es.emerging_score, COUNT(DISTINCT s.call_id) AS n_calls, SUM(CASE WHEN s.min_sentiment < 0 THEN -s.min_sentiment ELSE 0 END) AS neg_mass, SUM(CASE WHEN s.max_sentiment > 0 THEN s.max_sentiment ELSE 0 END) AS pos_mass, AVG(CASE WHEN th.polarity = 'positive' THEN s.max_sentiment ELSE s.min_sentiment END) AS mean_sentiment FROM themes th JOIN v_theme_call_sentiment s ON s.theme_id = th.theme_id JOIN calls c ON c.call_id = s.call_id LEFT JOIN emerging_scores es ON es.entity_type = 'theme' AND es.entity_id = th.theme_id AND es.as_of_week = ? WHERE 1=1 AND th.status = 'active' AND COALESCE(th.grouping_quality, 'ok') != 'weak' GROUP BY th.theme_id HAVING n_calls >= ? ORDER BY th.n_wordings DESC, th.theme_id LIMIT ?
SELECT tc.theme_id, tc.call_id FROM v_theme_calls tc JOIN calls c ON c.call_id = tc.call_id WHERE 1=1 AND tc.theme_id IN (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?) ORDER BY c.date DESC, tc.call_id
